title: Consumer Search and Social Learning in Agentic Markets
claim: A marketplace and agents jointly search and verify candidates, and inspection outcomes feed back to update shared beliefs.
layout: Single panel, numbered steps 1-5 looping clockwise; dashed feedback arrow on right
description: A single-panel illustrative diagram of an agent-assisted catering search, with five numbered steps in blue and teal. At left, a consumer icon has a speech bubble reading 'Caterer for 40 on Saturday; one guest has a sesame allergy' (step 1). An arrow leads to a blue robot labelled 'Personal agent'. A double arrow goes up to a 'Marketplace' box that suggests caterers A and B from prior feedback (step 2). Step 3, agent-to-agent checking, links the personal agent through a question bubble to two storefront icons with sales agents. Caterer A says its sauce contains sesame and gets a red FAIL tag. Caterer B offers a sesame-free menu and gets a green PASS tag. Step 4 is the recommendation back to the consumer. A dashed arrow on the right (step 5) returns to the marketplace and contrasts aggregate feedback ('A fails inspection') with screen-level feedback ('A fails dietary check').
caption: {Illustrative agent-assisted search and market learning. A marketplace uses prior feedback to suggest caterers; agent-to-agent conversations check their fit. Inspection outcomes update beliefs for subsequent consumers. Aggregate feedback reports whether inspection passed, whereas screen-level feedback identifies which checks passed or failed. Post-transaction quality feedback is omitted.}
abstract: Motivated by agentic markets -- where AI tools facilitate search -- we propose a model of consumer search and market-wide learning. A sequence of consumers engage in costly search to acquire progressively refined signals of product fit prior to purchase. The market observes acquired signals and post-transaction feedback thereby impacting future searches. We solve for the per-consumer optimal search policy and characterize the steady-state of the learning dynamics. Search technologies (agentic or otherwise) that reduce costs at fixed inspection depth improve long-run learning and consumer surplus. In a special case with screen-level feedback, more informative search also improves these outcomes. In contrast, we show through counterexamples and numerical simulations that more informative search can degrade long-run learning and consumer surplus when the market observes only aggregate inspection and transaction feedback, highlighting the importance of feedback design.
